title: The Best Expense Tracker Is the One You’ll Actually Use
text: Medium The Best Expense Tracker Is the One You’ll Actually Use | by Anvayasharma | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The only moment that matters What I built The decisions that made it stick What changed when friction disappeared The broader point Anvayasharma Always Growing Anvayasharma Always Growing Press enter or click to view image in full size Product Management Personal Finance Productivity Software Development Artificial Intelligence The Best Expense Tracker Is the One You’ll Actually Use Anvayasharma 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share I have tried every reasonable way to track my expenses. Dedicated budgeting apps. Notion templates. Spreadsheets with color-coded categories and monthly formulas. Each attempt followed the same arc: two weeks of diligent logging, a few days of guilt-skipping, and then quiet abandonment. The problem was never the tool. The tools were fine. The problem was that every one of them made the moment of logging feel like a chore. Open the app. Tap the plus button. Pick a category from a dropdown. Type the amount. Add a note. Save. That’s six steps for something that should feel like a reflex. It took me an embarrassingly long time to realize that this wasn’t a discipline problem. It was a design problem. Press enter or click to view image in full size The only moment that matters Most expense tracking products compete on what happens after you’ve logged your data. Better charts. Smarter budgets. Prettier breakdowns by category. But none of that matters if the data never gets entered in the first place. The bottleneck isn’t analysis. It’s capture. And the result of high-friction capture is predictable. You log the big stuff (rent, flights, subscriptions) and skip the small stuff (coffee, auto, snacks). Your data is structurally incomplete, and the entire system slowly becomes useless. Not because it broke, but because you stopped feeding it. I wanted logging an expense to feel closer to sending a text than filling out a form. And I wanted my data to land somewhere I already knew how to read: a spreadsheet. What I built I built a Telegram bot. You message it like you’d message a person, and it turns your message into a structured row in a Google Sheet. You type: flight 8977 delhi trip The bot replies: Logged: Flight | 8977 | Delhi trip | 25 Jun No app to open. No form to fill. No category to select. If you mention a date (“june 28”), it logs to that date. If you don’t, it defaults to today. Each month gets its own tab in the sheet, created automatically. Under the hood, the bot sends every message to a language model for parsing. The model reads your freeform text and extracts four things: category, amount, note, and date. It returns a small structured object, and the bot writes that as a row to your sheet. This means there’s no fixed format to memorize. “lunch 450,” “450 lunch,” “had lunch for 450 near office” all resolve to the same entry. You don’t adapt to the tool. The tool adapts to you. Press enter or click to view image in full size The data lands in Google Sheets because that’s where I was already comfortable looking at my finances. You can open your sheet anytime, see every entry, edit anything, add your own formulas. The sheet is the entire review UI, and it’s a UI you already know. Queries work the same way. Type “total this month” and the bot tells you. “Show flights” lists every flight entry. For open-ended questions, the bot reads your recent data and answers in plain text. No dashboards. Just ask. The whole thing runs on a single webhook endpoint. Telegram pushes your message to a small server, the server calls the language model, writes to your sheet, and replies. No session state, no database, no background processes. The architecture is almost comically simple, and that’s the point. Press enter or click to view image in full size The decisions that made it stick What I want to talk about isn’t the bot itself. It’s the tradeoffs behind it. Each one goes against conventional product logic, and each one is why this tool stuck where others didn’t. I put it in a chat, not an app. The most underrated quality of a chat interface is that it’s already open. I’m already in Telegram talking to people. The expense bot is just another conversation in my list. The context switch cost is zero. A dedicated app means leaving what you’re doing, finding the app, waiting for it to load, and starting a workflow. By the time you’ve done all that, the moment has passed. I used a language model instead of a form. A traditional app gives you fields: amount, category, date, notes. A form is unambiguous, but it’s also slow and rigid. The language model lets me type the way I think. I don’t have to decompose my expense into four fields. I just describe it the way I’d tell a friend: “auto 250 to office.” The cognitive cost of translating a thought into a form is real, and it’s the kind of micro-friction that kills daily habits. I stored data in a spreadsheet, not a database. This is the decision people question most. But a database requires a UI on top of it, and I didn’t want to build one. Google Sheets is the UI. I was already comfortable tracking finances in a spreadsheet. The bot just removed the part I hated: manually typing rows. The data format didn’t change. The entry method did. I left out budgeting, charts, and alerts. Every expense app ships with budgeting features. I deliberately didn’t. Not because budgeting is useless, but because it’s the wrong thing to optimize first. If the tool can’t get me to log consistently, no amount of budgeting logic matters. I wanted the product to do one thing well: capture expenses at the speed of thought. What changed when friction disappeared When logging takes three seconds and requires no app switch, you log everything. The 30-rupee chai. The 15-rupee parking.
